newsitem.title: INDIA: British Labour Party cautious on single currency.
newsitem.headline: British Labour Party cautious on single currency.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party would not take Britain into the European Monetary Union until the economy was ready for it, a senior party official said on Monday.

"It is possible to be positive of Britain's place in Europe while at the same time recognising that there are a few economic problems posed by the single currency project," Robin Cook, the party's foreign affairs spokesman, said in New Delhi.
"We believe that if you are going to have a single market, it would work better with a single currency," Cook told a news conference at the end of his first five-day visit to India.
But he said Britain could gain from the advantages of a single currency only if its economy could compete with other Eurpean allies.

"That is why ... we will join only after we are satisfied that we have achieved a convergence of real economic performance in the world of industrial output, investment, innovation and containment of unit costs," Cook said.
"At the moment I have to say that after 17 years of Conservative (Party) mismanagement in the economy, some of these questions are very difficut to answer."
Cook's views echoed the official Labour line on EMU but the party, like the Conservatives, appears to be having some difficulty in presenting a united front on the issue.
Cook said his party expects Prime Minister John Major to call general elections in spring next year. According to the constitution, polls must be held by May 22, 1997.

"While I have been in India an opinon poll has been published in Britain which puts Labour on 56 per cent and the Conservatives on 28 per cent," Cook said. "We are confident there will be a Labour government by the middle of next year."
A first round of European Economic and Monetary Union is scheduled for January 1, 1999.
Cook said a Labour government would take a decision on the issue by the end of 1997.
"I am very confident that Labour's industrial strategy will start to make a difference very quickly. But in terms of a timetable we face two different positions," he said.

"One is, some time towards the end of next year when a British government, which ever it is, will have to decide whether or not we will be joining the first wave. We say we will examine the books when we are elected, look at the figures, and make a decison then," he added
"In the longer term I think it will be very difficult for Britain to stay out indefinitely. And that is a matter we may have to come to in a medium term."
